raw_case_text: A 28-year-old Nigerian woman with a 20-week intrauterine pregnancy presented to the University of Florida Health Emergency Department (ED) with a five-day history of fever, diffuse joint pain, night sweats, vomiting, and malaise. She had arrived in the US to visit her family about nine days before her admission. She was initially diagnosed with cystitis and Streptococcus pyogenes throat infection and discharged with cephalexin for treatment. Her symptoms worsened, and she returned three days later to the ED for evaluation. On physical exam, she was afebrile, tachycardic, tachypneic, and hypotensive. Pertinent initial labs demonstrated hypoproliferative anemia (hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, was 11 g/dL three days prior, reticulocyte count 0.5%), thrombocytopenia (platelets 39,000/mm3, was 101,000/mm3 three days prior), D-dimer of 10.04 mug/mL, and LDH 341 U/L. Total bilirubin was 1.2 mg/dl. Complete blood count led to the evaluation of peripheral smear in which numerous inclusion bodies were noted (Figure 1). On further history, she confirmed that she discontinued her malaria prophylaxis, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, due to emesis associated with her pregnancy. A thick blood smear was prepared and showed evidence of malaria parasites, and her BiNax NOW  test was positive for P. falciparum. Her thin blood smears (Figure 2) demonstrated a parasitemia calculated at 9.8%, and thus, the patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring. Oral clindamycin and quinine were initiated until the CDC delivered intravenous artesunate, which was then continued. Her hospitalization was complicated by significant hypoglycemia requiring 5% dextrose infusion, and severe dyspnea was thought to be due to pulmonary edema requiring intravenous furosemide diuresis. CTA was negative for pulmonary embolism. The first dose of artesunate was given at 18:45 hours on day 2, and by 12:00 on day three, the parasite load was 0.09%. Patient completed four doses of IV artesunate and seven days of oral clindamycin. After the 4th dose of artesunate, no blood parasites were seen on peripheral smear (Figure 3). The patient was discharged home after a nine-day hospitalization with improvement in her anemia and thrombocytopenia. Upon clinic follow-up a few weeks later, the patient did not have any further complications associated with either her disease or therapy, with normal labs and an uncomplicated remainder of her pregnancy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old pregnant female at 20 weeks of gestation presenting with fever, joint pain, night sweats, and vomiting for five days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, a 28-year-old pregnant woman at 20 weeks of gestation, presented with a 5-day history of fever, arthralgias, nocturnal diaphoresis, vomiting, and malaise. Three days prior, she had presented to the emergency department, where she was diagnosed with cystitis and streptococcal pharyngitis and prescribed cephalexin. Her symptoms worsened significantly despite antibiotics, prompting re-presentation with worsening weakness and lightheadedness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Intrauterine pregnancy at 20 weeks of gestation. Epidemiological history: Arrived in the United States from Nigeria nine days prior to admission; had discontinued prescribed malaria chemoprophylaxis (trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole) due to pregnancy-related emesis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, night sweats, generalized joint pain, nausea, vomiting, and malaise; negative for rash, chest pain, or focal neurological deficits.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile, hypotensive, tachycardic, and tachypneic. Obstetric exam: Gravid uterus consistent with 20 weeks of gestation. During hospitalization, developed acute tachypnea and respiratory distress with bilateral pulmonary crackles consistent with pulmonary edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL (acute decline from 11.0 g/dL three days earlier), reticulocyte count 0.5% (hypoproliferative response); platelet count 39,000/mm3 (declined from 101,000/mm3); D-dimer 10.04 microg/mL; LDH 341 U/L; total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL. Hospital course notable for documented hypoglycemia on serum glucose monitoring.
objective.advanced_workup: CT pulmonary angiography (CTA): Negative for acute pulmonary embolism, showing pulmonary edema.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria in pregnancy (20 weeks gestation) complicated by hyperparasitemia (9.8%), hypotension, severe thrombocytopenia, non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and hypoglycemia. BinaxNOW rapid antigen test was positive for P. falciparum, and thick and thin blood smears demonstrated P. falciparum ring forms with 9.8% parasitemia.
Plan & Outcome: Admitted to the intensive care unit. Initiated on oral quinine and clindamycin, transitioning to CDC-provided intravenous artesunate (4 doses total) plus oral clindamycin for 7 days. Hypoglycemia was treated with intravenous 5% dextrose infusion, and acute pulmonary edema was successfully managed with IV furosemide diuresis. Parasitemia dropped to 0.09% within 18 hours of first artesunate dose, and smears were completely negative after the fourth dose. Discharged on hospital day 9 with normalized hematologic parameters and healthy fetal status.
